project.title: Smart Resume Analyzer
project.short_description: An explainable resume job matching service that scores a resume against a job description using SBERT sentence embeddings, breaks the score down requirement by requirement, flags skill gaps and ATS formatting issues, and benchmarks its ranking quality on 8,000 labelled resume job pairs.
project.overview: Smart Resume Analyzer compares a resume with a job description by meaning, not just keywords. It returns an overall match score built from four transparent components (skills, requirement coverage, experience relevance, education), marks every required skill as matched, related or missing, pairs each job requirement with the resume sentence that best supports it, and runs ten ATS formatting checks. A recruiter mode ranks up to 25 resumes against one job, and an optional LLM coach suggests learning resources and rewrites weak bullet points without inventing facts. The project went through two versions: v1 was a single Streamlit script; v2 rebuilt it as a tested FastAPI service with a Streamlit client, a hosted demo and a formal evaluation.
project.problem_statement:
Keyword-based applicant tracking systems reject candidates over wording: a resume that says “built dashboards” can miss a job description asking for “data visualization.” Candidates also get a single opaque score with no indication of what to fix. The goal was a tool that
(1) matches on meaning as well as keywords,
(2) explains its score at the level of individual skills and requirements, and
(3) is honestly evaluated on how well it actually ranks candidates.
project.dataset_info:
• App input: resumes uploaded as PDF or DOCX (including resumes laid out as Word tables) and a pasted job description.
  • Skill taxonomy: a hand-curated taxonomy of about 190 skills across 9 categories, each with its spelling variants and “substitute” groups (e.g. MySQL counts as related to PostgreSQL). Matching respects symbols and case, so C++, C#, CI/CD and S3 are recognised and “excellent” is not read as Excel.
  • Evaluation benchmark: cnamuangtoun/resume-job-description-fit on Hugging Face — 8,000 resume–job pairs labelled Good Fit, Potential Fit or No Fit. 6,241 pairs (280 jobs) for training and 1,759 pairs (71 jobs) for testing, with no job in both splits. The dataset text had lost most line breaks, which I partly repaired before evaluation. A key finding: 476 of the 477 test resumes also appear in the training split, paired with other jobs.
project.methodology:
1. Unit splitting: both documents are split into sentence-sized units (one per bullet or sentence), so the whole resume is read even though the embedding model only reads 256 tokens at a time.
  2. Embedding and similarity: each unit is embedded with SBERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and every resume unit is compared with every job unit by cosine similarity. Raw similarities are stretched onto 0–100 between a floor (0.15) and a ceiling (0.70).
  3. Four-component score:
    • Skills match (40%) — share of the job’s skills found; a related skill earns half credit.
    • Requirement coverage (30%) — best-matching resume unit for each job requirement, averaged.
    • Experience relevance (20%) — the five Experience/Projects statements that best match the job, averaged.
    • Education (10%) — degree level meets, is one level short of, or misses the requirement.
    A component that can’t be assessed is dropped and the remaining weights renormalised, rather than counting it as zero.
  4. Evaluation protocol: ranking quality is measured as AUC within each job (chance a Good Fit candidate ranks above a No Fit one), with 95% bootstrap intervals that resample whole jobs. Because resumes repeat across splits, I added a leakage check and a stricter unseen-resume protocol: four folds of resumes, each test pair scored by a model trained without its resume. All model selection used cross-validation on the training split only; the test split was used only to report.
  5. Compared methods: TF-IDF baseline, v1 whole-document SBERT cosine, v2 hand-weighted score, logistic regression / gradient boosting / pairwise rankers on sentence-level interaction features, and an SBERT bi-encoder fine-tuned for one epoch with triplet loss on (job, Good Fit resume, No Fit resume).
project.implementation_details:
• Architecture: Streamlit UI → FastAPI backend → core/ analysis package → Groq API (optional coach). The frontend holds no ML code and talks to the backend only over HTTP; core/ has no web-framework code, so it is testable and reusable on its own.
  • Core modules: PDF/DOCX parsing (pypdf, python-docx), section detection, NLTK-based sentence splitting, taxonomy skill extraction, degree-level detection, scoring with per-component explanations, ATS checks, PDF report generation (fpdf2), and an LLM client with model fallback.
  • ATS format check: ten rule-based checks — contact details that exist only as hyperlinks, icons that extract as junk, missing standard sections, length, unquantified or passive bullets, first-person pronouns.
  • Features: recruiter mode (rank up to 25 resumes with CSV export; unreadable files are skipped, not fatal), SQLite history with score change since the last analysis for the same job, downloadable PDF reports, unguessable share links, and an AI coach that leaves [placeholders] instead of inventing figures.
  • REST API: 11 endpoints (analyze, rank, history, reports, share links, coach) with interactive OpenAPI docs.
  • Engineering: two-container Docker Compose setup, pinned dependencies, environment-based configuration, per-visitor rate limiting for the coach, 185 pytest tests, and GitHub Actions CI running ruff lint and tests on every push.
  • Deployment: hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, running the API in-process with a CPU-only PyTorch build; public-demo settings isolate each visitor’s history and cap coach usage.
project.results:
On the stricter unseen-resume protocol (AUC within each job, 95% CI):

  • TF-IDF keyword baseline: 0.606 (0.539 – 0.676)
  • v1 whole document SBERT: 0.641 (0.584 – 0.702)
  • v2 hand weighted score (used in the app): 0.632 (0.566 – 0.703)
  • Logistic regression on v2’s sentence level features: 0.668 (0.598 – 0.741)
  • SBERT fine-tuned on the training split: 0.698 (0.627 – 0.772)
project.future_improvements:
• Show the fine-tuned model’s fit score in the app beside the explainable breakdown.
  • User accounts so history persists across visits.
  • Expand the skill taxonomy beyond tech roles, or learn skill relations instead of hand-curating them.
  • Judge education by field of study, not only degree level.
  • Support multi-column PDFs in reading order and scanned PDFs via OCR.
  • Validate against real hiring outcomes and a dataset with documented labels and licence.
project.my_role: I designed and built the project end to end as a solo project: the scoring method, the skill taxonomy, the parsing and section-detection pipeline, the FastAPI backend and Streamlit frontend, Docker and CI setup, the public deployment, and the evaluation study, including the leakage analysis and the fine-tuning experiment.
project.key_learnings:
• How easily data leakage inflates results: a model can look strong by recognising repeated resumes rather than reading the job, and catching that required designing a leakage check and a separate group-aware protocol.
  • Why confidence intervals and paired differences matter more than point scores when the test set is small.
  • That explainability and ranking accuracy are different goals; a transparent score can be useful without beating a simpler baseline, and saying so is part of honest reporting.
  • Structuring an ML application as a framework-independent core, an API and a thin client, with tests and CI, instead of a single script.
  • Constraining an LLM for factual safety (no invented numbers, placeholders instead) and the privacy trade-offs of sending text to a third-party API.
  • Practical deployment constraints: CPU-only builds, cold starts, per-visitor history isolation and rate limits on a free host.
